newsitem.title: USA: U.S. presidents pledge help for disadvantaged kids.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presidents pledge help for disadvantaged kids.

text.p: Standing in the shadow of the cradle of U.S. democracy, three presidents and a star-studded supporting cast on Monday urged an outpouring of civic activism to help disadvantaged young people learn and thrive.

"We gather here to pledge that those of us who are more fortunate will not forget those who are less fortunate," retired Gen. Colin Powell, chairman of the "Presidents' Summit for America's Future" and a prospective presidential candidate, said.
"Let's go save our children!" he declared, sounding the battlecry of the bipartisan summit that opened on Sunday and winds up on Tuesday.

On a chilly, overcast day that held down the turnout for the ceremony in the square in front of historic Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution were adopted, President Bill Clinton and former presidents George Bush and Gerald Ford -- a Democrat and two Republicans -- signed "America's Promise" to its youth.

The pact, signed for incapacitated former President Ronald Reagan by his wife Nancy, commits them to encourage a new era of community service that will get corporate America and plain citizens to see that two million underprivileged young people have mentors and role models by 2000.
Former Democratic President Jimmy Carter, who took part in a summit-related Philadelphia neighbourhood cleanup on Sunday, had a prior commitment and did not attend the signing.

While the leaders were speaking, several hundred union members and social activists began a day-long "People's Summit" at a nearby park. The event aims to protest welfare cuts and call for the government to create jobs and provide health care, organisers and participants said.

Clinton, who during the 1992 presidential campaign belittled Bush's "Points of Light" programme to encourage volunteerism, said the new emphasis on community service was part of the country's unending effort to improve living conditions for every citizen.

"Yes, there are things that the government should do ..." Clinton said. "But even if we do everything we should, you and I know that a lot of the problems facing our children are problems of the human heart."
He said those problems "can only be solved when there is a one-on-one connection, community by community, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, street by street, home by home, with every child in America."
